post.title: Above Ireland
post.body:
I lived in Ireland for nine years. These photos are from two days of drone flights around County Donegal in July 2018, all taken from above.

## The coast near Ards Friary, straight down

The first set is from the afternoon of July 10, a little after four, on the coast near Ards Friary. The water was the surprise: clear turquoise over pale sand, with dark patches of rock and weed showing right through it. Straight down, the coastline turned into pattern. A grey cliff edge with heather on top. A narrow cave cut back into the rock, green water running into it. A small sandy cove between two dark arms of stone.

One frame looks out instead of down: a thin paved path winding along a green headland, rocky shore on one side, open water and low hills across the bay under a grey sky.

> Straight down, the coastline turned into pattern.

## A ring of stone

Six days later, on the morning of July 16, just before eleven, I flew over Grianán of Aileach, the round stone fort on a hilltop. From the side it is a thick ring wall with terraces stepping down the inside. From straight above it becomes a near-perfect circle sitting in brown heather, with a path running up to its one doorway. Pull back far enough and it is a small grey ring in a patchwork of fields, with water spreading out in the distance.

The people walking around it are tiny in these shots, which is what tells you how big it is.

## Two pictures of one place

What I learned: the same place can be two different pictures. Looking straight down turns a coastline or a fort into a shape; tilting the camera up to the horizon puts it back into the landscape. Both are worth taking.

episode.title: The ring on the hill
episode.script:
Narrated by Robot Marley.

It was July, in Ireland, a little after four in the afternoon, and the sky was the soft grey that sky there often is.

Christian lived in Ireland for nine years. These pictures come from two days of drone flights over County Donegal. Straight down, mostly. And straight down, the coast near Ards Friary stopped looking like a coast and started looking like a painting.

The water was clear enough to see through. Pale turquoise over sand, with dark shapes of rock and weed lying under it like shadows. Along one edge ran a grey cliff with heather growing on top. A little farther on, a narrow cave cut back into the rock, and the green water followed it in.

Then Christian tilted the camera up. A thin path wound along a green headland, the rocky shore on one side, the open bay and low hills on the other. It is a quiet picture. It is also a very good one, because he let the path lead the eye all the way to the water.

***

Six days later, just before eleven in the morning, the drone went up over a hill called GREE-nawn of AWE-ul-yok.

On top sat a ring of stone. A thick round wall, with terraces stepping down the inside like seats around a green floor. A path came up the hill to a single small doorway.

Here is the part I like. Christian took it from the side, so you could see the wall and the steps. Then he took it from straight above, and it became a nearly perfect circle sitting in the brown heather. Then he pulled back, and back again, until the whole fort was a small grey ring in a patchwork of fields, with water spreading out toward the horizon.

The people walking around it were tiny. That was the point. Without them, you would never guess how big it was.

Knowing when to look down and when to look out is most of what a good eye is.

***

Two days, a coastline and a circle of stone. Some places look best from the ground. These, it turned out, looked best from above.
